title: Peaceful and wrathful
hookLine: the visions of the bardo, recognized as the mind's own display
last: THE CLEAR LIGHT IS YOUR OWN MIND.

cards: Inside a Tibetan temple, the wall paintings go all the way around. On one side, calm figures sit on lotuses, gentle faces, soft colors, hands resting in their laps.

A few steps along, the mood changes: dark blue and red bodies, flaming hair, bared teeth, crowns of skulls, a stance like they're about to stamp the ground. It feels like a walk from a garden into a storm.
Both walls belong to the same teaching. In the Tibetan texts of the in-between, these are the figures that appear after death, and the instruction that comes with them is short and startling.

teach.b: The Bardo Thodol, known in English as the Tibetan Book of the Dead, describes what the one who has died meets in the in-between. If the clear light passes unrecognized, visions follow.
First come peaceful figures, buddhas of light, radiant and kind. Then, as the text tells it, the same figures return in wrathful form, fierce and terrifying. Here's the surprise.
The text doesn't tell the dead person to fight these beings, or run, or plead with them.
It says, again and again: recognize them. They are not visitors from outside.

teach.h: FIERCE IS COMPASSION, NOT A DEMON.
teach.b: They are the display of your own mind, the calm ones and the fierce ones alike. Why fierce at all? In Tibetan teaching, a wrathful figure is not a demon.
It is compassion with its sleeves rolled up: the energy that cuts through confusion, the way a parent shouts when a child steps toward a road.
The fierceness is aimed at what blocks waking up, never at the one who's waking. Some teachers in this tradition point out that people live through small versions of this all the time.

teach.h: A MOOD ON AN ORDINARY DAY.
teach.b: A mood rises, gentle or furious, and it seems to come from out there: the email, the driver, the weather. The bardo teaching asks a simpler question first.
Whose mind is showing this? Recognition, the text says, is enough. Some readers take the visions quite literally; others hear them mainly as a map of the mind.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, peaceful and wrathful figures appear in temple paintings and in the bardo texts, and teachers explain them as forms of awakened mind that the dead, and the living, are asked to recognize rather than fear.

o: good spirits and evil demons who judge the dead
calm and fierce figures seen as the mind's own display
two moods a monk must choose between in meditation

games.q: peaceful and wrathful: tap the pairs.
p: compassion with its sleeves rolled up

s: the wrathful figures are demons to be fought
the text asks the dead to recognize them as the display of their own mind, not to fight them.
in the text, the peaceful figures appear before the wrathful ones
if the clear light passes unrecognized, peaceful visions come first, then fierce ones.
the text asks the dead to run from the fierce visions
it asks, again and again, for recognition. recognition, it says, is enough.

games.q: you're in the in-between, and a terrifying figure with flaming hair rises in front of you. the text is being read to you. what does it tell you to do?
o: recognize it as your own mind's display.
beg it to leave you alone.
games.why: the text's instruction is recognition: the fierce figures, like the calm ones, are the mind's own display.

practice: Sit comfortably and wait for a mood to show up, calm, restless, irritated or sad; it doesn't need to be a big one. Don't push it away or follow its story, just name it quietly: this is a mood, and it's appearing in my mind.
If it changes into another mood, name that one too, peaceful or wrathful, each with the same plain recognition.

wordCard.voice: Peaceful and wrathful. The calm and fierce figures of the in-between, which the Tibetan text asks the dead to recognize as their own mind's display. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan zhi khro: zhi, peaceful, and khro, wrathful. The name for the deities of the bardo.

carryVoice: Your line: your own mind. The calm faces and the fierce ones, both. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: the bardo of reality: the peaceful and wrathful deities, and the instruction to recognize them
sources.work: Bardo Thodol (Liberation through Hearing in the Between), attributed to Padmasambhava
